lessons.title: Why Technology Roadmapping Is Collaborative, Cross-Industry Planning
lessons.description: This lesson introduces the foundational concepts of technology roadmapping as presented in the MIT Sloan seminar 15.795 during the Fall 2002 semester. It covers the systematic mapping of technological development paths, the collaborative nature of the planning process involving industry and research partners, and the rigorous expectations for students developing roadmap drafts. This lesson explores the institutional motivations and conceptual frameworks of technology roadmapping as presented in an introductory MIT Sloan seminar. It focuses on the integration of research into the student experience and the collaborative nature of strategic planning.

lessons.title: Organizing the Roadmapping Project: Teams, MiniMaps, and Shared Resources
lessons.description: This lesson covers the organizational framework of the seminar, focusing on the student-led team formation process, the expectations for professional self-management, and the initial MiniMap project used to catalyze collaboration and research. This lesson covers the final stages and resource framework of the Technology Roadmapping seminar as presented in the Fall 2002 orientation. It details the planned semester finale, the assembly of a roadmap compendium, and the network of MIT research contacts and sample readings available to students for their projects. This lesson establishes the norms for collaborative resource sharing and the mutual educational responsibilities of the participants.

lessons.title: Convex optimization versus local and global nonlinear optimization
lessons.description: This lesson explores the practical implementation and computational complexity of convex optimization, contrasting it with local and global methods for general nonlinear programming. We focus on the trade-offs between solution reliability, computational efficiency, and the conceptual challenge of problem formulation. This lesson explores the practical utility of convex optimization beyond its own domain, detailing its role in initializing local optimization, providing heuristics for nonconvex problems, and establishing bounds for global optimization. It also outlines the structural hierarchy of the textbook, moving from theoretical foundations and applications to the algorithmic hierarchy of linear equations, Newton's method, and interior-point methods. This lesson covers the foundational notation and mathematical conventions used throughout the study of convex optimization, including set definitions, vector/matrix representations, generalized inequalities, and function domains as presented on physical PDF pages 28 and 29.

lessons.title: Affine geometry, convex combinations, convex hulls, and cones
lessons.description: This lesson covers the fundamental geometric structures used in convex optimization, including lines, line segments, affine sets, and the concept of relative interior, based on physical PDF pages 35 through 37 of Convex Optimization. This lesson explores the fundamental geometric structures of convex sets, convex hulls, and various types of cones. We transition from simple line segments to generalized expectations and conic combinations, supported by visual examples and rigorous algebraic verifications.

lessons.title: Canonical convex sets: halfspaces, ellipsoids, norm cones, polyhedra, and the PSD cone (pages 41–48)
lessons.description: Page-aligned instructor narration that restates and clarifies the algebraic forms, assumptions, and geometric interpretations from Boyd & Vandenberghe (physical pages 41–48). Each section preserves the source's equation numbering and matrix/ordering assumptions, makes explicit the convex-cone language required by the plan, and highlights where a small 2×2 canonical PSD boundary formula appears immediately after the assigned page range (p.49) so instructors can choose to present it as a sourced extension or an independent worked example. Includes worked examples and practice tasks for learners.

lessons.title: Generalized inequalities and separating/supporting hyperplanes
lessons.description: A university-level exploration of proper cones, the partial orderings they induce, and the distinction between minimum and minimal elements in convex sets based on physical PDF pages 57 through 59 of Convex Optimization. This lesson covers the distinction between minimum and minimal elements in convex sets and provides a detailed proof of the Separating Hyperplane Theorem for disjoint convex sets. This lesson explores the geometric and algebraic foundations of separating and supporting hyperplanes within convex sets. We cover the conditions for strict separation, the converse of the separating hyperplane theorem, and the application of these concepts to systems of linear inequalities via the theorem of alternatives.

lessons.title: Dual cones and dual-order tests
lessons.description: This lesson covers the fundamental concepts of supporting hyperplanes and dual cones as presented in physical PDF pages 65 through 67. We explore the geometric and algebraic definitions of dual cones, examine specific examples like the positive semidefinite cone and norm cones, and conclude with the application of dual generalized inequalities in convex optimization. This lesson covers the application of dual cones to generalized inequalities, including theorems of alternatives for strict inequalities and the dual characterization of minimum and minimal elements in both convex and non-convex sets. lessons.description: This lesson introduces the foundational concepts of Lagrangian duality, defining the Lagrangian and the Lagrange dual function, and establishing how the dual function provides lower bounds on the optimal value of an optimization problem. lessons.title: Projection, separation, and distance between convex sets
lessons.description: This lesson covers the mathematical foundations of projecting points onto sets, the conditions for uniqueness of such projections, and the relationship between projection and the separation of convex sets using hyperplanes. We explore analytical solutions for polyhedra, rectangles, and cones, alongside the optimization formulations that define these geometric operations. This lesson covers the geometric and optimization-based foundations of projecting points onto convex sets, constructing separating hyperplanes via Lagrange duality, and defining the distance between two convex sets. We explore these concepts using Euclidean norms, general norms, and functional representations like indicator and support functions. This lesson covers physical PDF pages 417 through 418 of Convex Optimization, focusing on the mathematical formulation of the distance between convex sets, the dual interpretation of this distance as a separating hyperplane, and the introduction of indicator functions in these geometric problems.

lessons.title: Euclidean distance/angle models and extremal ellipsoids
lessons.description: This lesson covers the representation of geometric configurations using Gram matrices, the conditions for realizability of distances and angles, and the formulation of these geometric properties as convex optimization problems. This lesson explores the geometric applications of convex optimization, specifically focusing on how to model configurations of vectors using Gram matrices, correlation coefficients, and Euclidean distance matrices. It also introduces the concept of extremal volume ellipsoids, specifically the Löwner-John ellipsoid, which is the minimum volume ellipsoid covering a given set. This lesson covers the formulation of extremal volume ellipsoids, specifically focusing on the Löwner-John ellipsoid which encloses a given set. We explore how to calculate these ellipsoids for polyhedra and unions of ellipsoids, and we examine the efficiency of these ellipsoidal approximations for general and symmetric convex sets. This lesson covers the mathematical formulation and properties of maximum volume inscribed ellipsoids within convex sets, specifically polyhedra and intersections of ellipsoids, as well as their approximation efficiency and affine invariance.

lessons.title: Building Probability Models: Sample Spaces, Events, Axioms, and Additivity
lessons.description: This lesson introduces the foundational components of a probabilistic model, focusing on the definition of experiments, the criteria for valid sample spaces, and the visual and mathematical representation of discrete and continuous outcomes. This lesson covers the transition from individual outcomes to events, the fundamental axioms of probability, and the derivation of key properties such as the probability of complements and finite additivity. This university-level instructional narration, based on physical PDF pages 9 through 11 of the provided transcript, explains the application of probability axioms to discrete and continuous models. It covers the discrete uniform law using a four-sided die example, the uniform area law for continuous sample spaces, and introduces the conceptual need for extending additivity by presenting an infinite coin-tossing waiting-time model. This lesson examines the transition to unbounded discrete sample spaces, culminating in the formal definition of the Countable Additivity Axiom to justify infinite probability summations.

lessons.description: A page-aligned lesson explaining what the assigned physical PDF pages (249–255) actually print about benchmark datasets, competitions, and dataset roles, now augmented with explicit instructor commentary on leaderboard incentives/metric gaming and practical mitigation techniques. All page references are physical PDF page numbers; where this lecture adds practices or examples that are not printed on those pages, they are clearly labeled as instructor additions.

lessons.title: Datasets III: Scientific validity, leakage, harms, and documentation
lessons.description: This lesson explores the scientific foundations of machine learning benchmarks, focusing on the train-test paradigm, the risks of adaptive overfitting, and the cultural and technical practices that maintain the validity of these benchmarks. We also examine the influential role of dataset creators in defining research agendas through task selection and domain abstraction. This lesson explores the scientific and ethical responsibilities of dataset creators and users, focusing on the mechanics of data leakage, the culture of benchmarking, and the various forms of harm that arise from dataset properties and distribution. This lesson explores systematic methods for dataset documentation, the influence of archival sciences on data curation, and the strategic necessity of separating scientific benchmark datasets from production-oriented training data to mitigate harm.

lessons.title: Datasets IV: Stewardship, validity, human comparisons, and limits of prediction
lessons.description: This lesson explores the ethical and technical governance of datasets, focusing on the distinction between scientific benchmarks and production datasets, the necessity of stewardship for dataset derivatives, and the application of measurement theory to target variables in machine learning. This lesson explores the conceptual frameworks for measuring the effectiveness of machine learning models, focusing on the distinction between reliability and validity. It examines the nuances of construct validity, the pitfalls of comparing machine performance to human baselines, and the limitations of optimizing for a single objective in complex real-world environments. This lesson examines the evolution of fairness-focused benchmarks, the risks of Goodhart’s Law in machine learning evaluation, and the fundamental limits of social prediction as illustrated by the Fragile Families Challenge. It concludes with a summary of the dataset framework presented throughout the chapter.

lessons.title: Vectors, matrix products, rank, and the CR factorization
lessons.description: An introduction to the three fundamental matrix factorizations and the basic principles of linear combinations, vector operations, and geometric spans in three-dimensional space. This lesson covers the fundamental operations of vector geometry and matrix algebra, focusing on dot products, lengths, angles, and the conceptual interpretations of matrix-vector multiplication. It also introduces the vital concepts of column space and row space, which form the foundation for understanding linear transformations and systems of equations. This lesson explores the foundational concepts of linear independence and dependence within matrix columns, the four distinct ways to interpret matrix multiplication, and the fundamental CR factorization that links column and row rank. This lesson explores the fundamental structure of rank-one matrices, their role as the building blocks of all matrices, and the foundational theorem that column rank equals row rank.

lessons.title: Solving square systems: inverses, elimination, pivoting, and LU
lessons.description: This lesson covers the fundamental methods for solving square linear systems, including the properties of inverse matrices, the mechanics of back substitution for triangular systems, and the process of Gaussian elimination to achieve LU decomposition. This lesson covers the practical mechanics of solving linear systems, focusing on row exchanges via permutation matrices, the rank-one construction of LU decomposition, and the properties of transposes and symmetric matrices.

lessons.title: Vector spaces, four fundamental subspaces, graph incidence, and pseudoinverses
lessons.description: This lesson explores the formal definition of vector spaces and subspaces, identifies the four fundamental subspaces associated with a matrix, and demonstrates how to use reduced row echelon form to determine bases and the column-row factorization. This lesson covers the construction of nullspace solutions from reduced row echelon form, the fundamental theorem of linear algebra regarding subspace dimensions, and the application of incidence matrices to graph theory and Kirchhoff's laws. This lesson explores the concept of the pseudoinverse (A plus), providing a generalized inverse for any matrix, regardless of its shape or rank. We examine how the pseudoinverse relates to the four fundamental subspaces and how it can be constructed using the Singular Value Decomposition (SVD).

lessons.title: Eigenanalysis, positive definiteness, differential equations, and second differences
lessons.description: This lesson covers the fundamental concepts of eigenvalues and eigenvectors, matrix diagonalization, and the properties of symmetric positive definite matrices as presented in Gilbert Strang's linear algebra notes. This lesson explores the application of eigenvalues and eigenvectors to linear differential equations, the stability of these systems, and the use of second-difference matrices in engineering contexts.

lessons.title: Singular value decomposition, PCA, computation, compression, and orthogonality
lessons.description: This lesson explores the Singular Value Decomposition (SVD), covering its mathematical definition, the distinction between reduced and full forms, its derivation from symmetric matrices, and its geometric interpretation as a rotate-stretch-rotate sequence. This lesson covers the theoretical foundations of matrix approximation via the Eckart-Young theorem, the practical application of Principal Component Analysis (PCA) for data variance, the iterative algorithms used to compute singular values, and the efficiency of SVD in image compression. This lesson synthesizes the fundamental role of orthogonality in linear algebra, covering geometric properties, matrix decompositions, and functional analysis as presented on physical PDF page 55.

lessons.title: Linear transformations, calculus matrices, complex spaces, Fourier transforms, convolution, and FFT
lessons.description: This lesson explores the fundamental definition of linear transformations, their application in calculus through derivative and integral matrices, and the general procedure for representing any linear transformation as a matrix relative to specific bases. This lesson explores the transition from real to complex vector spaces, defining complex arithmetic, polar representations, and the fundamental properties of complex matrices such as Hermitian and Unitary forms. This lesson covers the fundamentals of complex matrices, including Hermitian and unitary properties, the construction and scaling of the Fourier matrix, and the relationship between cyclic convolution and circulant matrices. This lesson explores the computational efficiency of the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) through the Cooley-Tukey block factorization, detailing how recursive halving and permutations reduce matrix multiplication complexity.

lessons.title: Learning from data: ReLU networks, optimization, CNNs, and backpropagation
lessons.description: This lesson explores the mathematical structure of neural networks using the Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU), the geometric complexity of the resulting learning functions, and the optimization techniques used to train these models. This lesson explores advanced topics in learning from data, focusing on improving gradient descent convergence with momentum, the architecture of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), and the mathematical foundations of backpropagation using the multivariable chain rule.

lessons.title: Basic statistics: distributions, covariance, concentration, and Markov chains
lessons.description: This lesson covers fundamental statistical concepts including the distinction between sample and population parameters, key probability distributions such as Binomial, Poisson, and Normal, and the mechanics of covariance matrices for multivariate data. This lesson covers fundamental statistical inequalities for bounding probabilities and introduces the theory and application of Markov matrices and chains, focusing on convergence to steady states.

sourceCoverage.title: Fairness and Machine Learning (Barocas, Hardt & Narayanan)
sourceCoverage.scopeNote: A 2023-compiled, 294-physical-page open educational textbook on fairness and machine learning. It covers institutional legitimacy, classification metrics and incompatibilities, normative theories, causality, a US anti-discrimination-law case study, empirical audits, structural discrimination/interventions, datasets, and a substantive structural-factors appendix. It is not a complete course syllabus, a turnkey fairness procedure, or current legal advice; the authors explicitly identify a US/Western orientation and foundational scope.
gaps: While the text introduces the assumption that predictions do not influence outcomes, it does not provide a mathematical framework on these pages for scenarios where this non-interference assumption is violated.
The detailed algorithms for supervised learning are intentionally omitted as the text states they are heuristics rather than the focus of this population-level foundational chapter.
The text mentions that researchers have proposed dozens of criteria, but only three are detailed here.
Statistical arguments for estimating probabilities from random samples are explicitly excluded as they are not the focus of the chapter.
The full normative debate regarding these definitions is deferred to Chapter 4 of the source text.

sourceCoverage.title: MIT 18.06 ZoomNotes for Linear Algebra
sourceCoverage.scopeNote: Gilbert Strang's 2021 ZoomNotes is a compact visual set of lecture notes spanning 11 parts: core linear algebra through SVD, transformations/Fourier analysis, learning from data, and basic statistics. It explicitly says it does not teach every topic in the cited textbooks. Although the closing footer identifies MIT OCW 18.06 Spring 2010 and the notes point to 18.06/18.065 resources, this PDF is its own concise notes source, not a complete substitute for either full course or the cited books.
gaps: The specific definition of 'rank' mentioned in the group title is not explicitly detailed on these pages, though the concept is illustrated through the dimension of the spaces (line vs plane).
The 'CR factorization' mentioned in the group title is not explained on physical pages 9 through 11.

The source mentions Parts 1, 3, 2, 4, 6, and 7 of the ZoomNotes for the five factorizations, but the specific details of LU, QR, Spectral, and SVD are not explained on this page beyond their identification as column-times-row sums.
The notes mention 'six 3 by 3 permutations' and ask if P1P2 = P2P1, but do not list the matrices or provide the answer (which is generally no, as matrix multiplication is non-commutative).
The notes refer to 'column-row multiplication (see 1.6)' which is outside the assigned page range.
The notes mention that pivots in U go into D for the LDU transpose form but do not show the explicit algebraic steps for extracting D from U.
The notes mention 'functions ax+b' as a vector space example but do not explicitly provide the basis or dimension for this specific function space on these pages.
The proof that all bases have the same number of vectors is presented as a summary sketch rather than a step-by-step formal derivation.
The specific regularity conditions for the Central Limit Theorem, such as the requirement for finite variance, are assumed in the text's compact phrasing but not explicitly listed.
The text mentions 'Bound for 2 delta equals (Bound for delta) to the fourth power' without providing a formal proof or further context for this specific scaling.
The specific calculation for the second eigenvalue lambda equals one half is not shown step-by-step; the value is simply stated.
No technical lecture content or mathematical theorems are present on these administrative pages.
The source page is a table of contents and does not contain the mathematical definitions, proofs, or numerical exercises for the listed sections.
The source page is strictly a table of contents; specific definitions, geometric explanations, and algorithms for the listed topics are not present on this physical page.
